paper_title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Given the current observation and a sequence of robot actions, a robotic world model predicts the future
video frames. Such models serve as learned surrogates of the real world in robot manipulation, where they
are used to evaluate policies, to plan actions and to synthesize training data [22, 41, 84, 96]. These uses
impose two requirements on the predicted video. The first is action following: the robot must execute the
given actions. The second is interaction fidelity: the objects in contact with the robot must respond as
they would in reality, whether they are carried, pushed, dragged, deformed or released, while preserving
their shape and identity.
sections.content: Early robotic world models encode the action as numeric vector, such as end-effector poses or joint angles [22, 84, 96], and leave the video model to infer from pixels both how the robot appears and how the scene responds. Recent work instead renders the robot into pixel-aligned conditions, such as masks, URDF renders or surface tracks [1, 2, 6, 35, 39]. This specifies the robots appearance in every frame and makes action following far more reliable, but interaction fidelity improves much less. As shown in Fig. 1b, objects may collapse during contact, as when slice of bread and the spatula dragging it come apart, or respond inconsistently with the action, as when released cup rises with the open gripper. We attribute these failures to the conditioning (Fig. 1a): an action, numeric or rendered, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, so single video model must infer the interaction dynamics implicitly Figure 1: Action-only conditioning leaves the scenes response to the video model. (a) simulator predicts how scene points respond, so the video model mainly renders this response. (b) Two DROID test clips: objects respond wrongly with action-only conditioning (robot render; red) but not with the proxy (green). while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering. This separation is inspired by code world models [12, 14], which evolve an explicit world state with program, render it into coarse proxy video, and let video model synthesize the final frames; physics-grounded video generation does the same with simulated physics [46, 69]. For robot manipulation, the central design choice is the proxy: it must represent arbitrary objects, including deformable and articulated ones, be obtainable from single real observation, and admit dynamics that can be predicted under robot actions. Physics simulators require physical parameters, object assets and object-specific solvers that are difficult to obtain in real scenes [47, 81], and hand-written rules cannot express pushing, dragging or deformation. We instead use 3D points as the proxy. Points represent any object without segmentation or model, can be lifted from single RGB-D frame, describe the robot and the scene in the same space, and their dynamics can be learned directly from real robot interaction data. With points as the proxy, the world model first simulates how the points move and then renders them into video  (Fig. 2)  . We lift the first frame into 3D scene points and convert the actions into robot points via forward kinematics. learned point dynamics model, the simulator, predicts how every scene point responds to the robots motion; we instantiate it with PointWorld [26]. The simulated points are rendered back, together with the robot, into pixel-aligned proxy videos, which video model, the renderer, reads through its own encoder and turns into realistic frames. The simulator thus decides what happens and the renderer decides how it looks, and each can be replaced independently. We study this design in controlled setting on the DROID dataset [34] with two renderers of different architectures, Wan2.2 [67] (DiT) and Ctrl-World [22] (UNet), comparing four conditions, each giving the video model more explicit information than the last: numeric action, robot render, robot render with depth, and the point dynamics proxy. We measure interaction fidelity by object motion error, computed from object points tracked in the generated and the real video rather than from image metrics dominated by the background, and repeat the study on real bimanual robot. Our experiments show that: Interaction fidelity improves. Against the robot render, the proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% on DROID, without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on the real robot. The gain concentrates on pushed, dragged and deformed objects (Sec. 4.2), and on the real robot on deformable ones (Sec. 4.5). The video follows the simulation. Object motion error decreases as the simulator improves, from points held static through hand-written rule to learned simulators, and editing the simulated motion steers the video (Sec. 4.3). 2 Point dynamics help more as input than as matched auxiliary loss. With the same data and training budget, point forcing, an auxiliary point-tracking loss following PhysisForcing [90], lowers object motion error by 3.4%, and the simulated point dynamics as input by 8.6% (Sec. 4.4).

sections.title:
2 Related Work
Robotic world models for manipulation. Robotic world models are increasingly built on large video
generation models [17, 22, 27, 29, 44, 51–53, 58, 76, 84, 96]. What such a model has to infer depends
on how the action is given. A numeric action leaves it to infer both where the robot goes and how the
scene responds. Rendering the robot into the frame as masks, meshes, skeletons, point maps, tracks or
flow [1, 2, 6, 16, 35, 36, 39, 65, 75, 83] settles the first question and makes action following far more reliable,
but not the second. A few models also receive a signal about the scene. Some take it as given, such as
simulated depth [24] or occupancy from reconstruction or simulation [85]; others predict it together with the
frames, as next-frame scene flow learned mostly in simulation [21] or as a low-resolution preview video [62].
Most work, however, keeps the scene’s response inside the video model. The model is post-trained on
counterfactual actions [40], off-expert actions [10] or its own rollouts with reinforcement learning [3].
Others make it generate depth, point maps or flow along with the frames [48, 68, 93, 94], or add auxiliary
losses on motion and geometry, first for general video generation [7, 31, 79, 92] and recently for robotic
world models [9, 30, 43, 74, 90, 95]. We compare one such loss with an explicit input in Sec. 4.4.
sections.content: Simulate, then render. Several lines of video generation keep how world evolves apart from how it looks. Code world models [12, 14] and game generators [28, 45] let program evolve the state and video model paint it. Physics-grounded generation does the same with physics simulator [8, 15, 42, 46, 47, 82, 91], learned physics model [69] or an evolving 4D scene state [70], whose renders, flow or tracks reach the video model as the signals already used to control motion and camera [1820, 61, 87]. Both stages can also be learned: language-model backbone evolves latent world state under actions, and video diffusion decoder renders it [54]. Three concurrent works are closest to ours, as they predict dynamics in 3D before rendering. DeXplicit models handobject interaction and needs object labels and canonical shapes [37]. 3D World Simulator fits particlevoxel dynamics and Gaussian renderer to each multi-camera workspace [71], and VPTwin simulates digital twin that VLM builds for each task [81]. Our intermediate is instead an explicit 3D point state, predicted from the actions by separately trained point model learned from real robot data, without object models, physical parameters or per-scene capture. Learned 3D dynamics. Learned dynamics models predict how particles, graphs or Gaussians move and deform under robot action, but are mostly fitted to one object or task [25, 32, 49, 88, 89], and object-centric variants assume segmented rigid or articulated parts [37, 77]. Scene-level point models drop these assumptions and scale to in-the-wild robot data [4, 13, 26, 38, 55, 56, 73, 86], and generative particle models are trained on large simulated corpora [11], including concurrent work [60]. These models predict the evolving 3D state rather than video. Because the proxy only needs per-point displacements, they could serve as our simulator; we use PointWorld [26], which is public and trained on real robot data, and vary its output at test time in Sec. 4.3.

3.1 Simulate-then-render formulation
A robotic world model predicts future observations o1:T from the first observation o0 and the robot’s
actions a0:T ; here o0 holds RGB-D images from calibrated cameras, and at is the robot’s joint configuration,
sections.content: 3 Figure 2: Overview. The first frame is lifted into scene points P0, and forward kinematics turns the actions into robot points Q0:T (light to dark blue over time). The simulator predicts how the scene points move (purple to yellow), Π renders them with the robot into three pixel-aligned proxy videos, and the renderer turns the proxy and the first frame into video. One of the two cameras is shown. including the gripper. We factorize the model into four steps: Q0:T = FK(cid:0)a0:T (cid:1), P1:T = S(cid:0)P0, Q0:T (cid:1), c0:T = Π(cid:0)o0, P0:T , Q0:T (cid:1), o1:T R(cid:0)o0, c0:T (cid:1). (1) Forward kinematics turns the actions into robot surface points Q0:T , the simulator predicts how the scene points P0 lifted from the first frame move in response, Π renders the 3D points into pixel-aligned proxy videos c0:T , and the renderer R, video model, turns the proxy into frames. In this factorization, the actions enter only through kinematics, so only the scenes response has to be predicted. Existing interfaces use only part of this chain. Numeric-action models [22, 84, 96] read the actions as vector, here the end-effector pose given by forward kinematics and the gripper. Robot-render models [1, 35, 39] receive rendering of the robot points Q0:T alone, and depth condition [24] adds the scenes geometry, here depth rendering of Q0:T over the dense scene points held in place, as if were the identity (Sec. 4.1). 3.2 3D state and simulator Each cameras depth map is back-projected into the robot base frame, without the pixels covered by the robot at t=0. Since the cost of simulation grows with the number of points and the quality of rendering with their density, the simulator receives sparse voxelized points P0 = {pj} merged over cameras, while the proxy uses dense points = {pi}, one per pixel of camera with its color. Robot points are sampled once on the URDF surface, proportionally to area, and placed at every frame by forward kinematics. The simulator predicts displacement pj,t for every scene point and step, and any model with this interface can serve as (Sec. 4.3). We instantiate with PointWorld-large [26], scene-level point dynamics model trained on DROID that reads the gripper points; on the real robot, we fine-tune it on our own recordings (Sec. 4.5). PointWorld describes each point, voxelized at 1.5 cm, by DINOv3 features [63] and predicts its displacement for 10 steps, one every two video frames, which we interpolate linearly in time. On real data such as DROID, it is trained on label point flow, pseudo-labels made of point tracks estimated in the video [33] and lifted to 3D with depth.

3.3 Point dynamics proxy
Rendering the points into pixel-aligned videos lets any video model read them through its own VAE. The
proxy sees the simulator only through the simulated points. It contains the robot render and adds the
scene’s geometry and its simulated response. For each camera, Π renders three videos by z-buffered point
splatting [78, 97], where each pixel shows the nearest projected point: the robot render crob, a warp cwarp

The moved dense points and the robot points share one z-buffer, so the arm, the objects it moves and the background occlude each other correctly, and pixels that no point reaches stay black to mark where new content must be generated. Tracks. The track video draws fixed subset of 4,000 simulated scene points and 1,500 robot points without spatial interpolation, each colored by its initial 3D position in the robot base frame [20]. dot keeps its color as it moves, so the renderer can follow each point across frames and views, and objects separate from their surroundings by moving differently, without segmentation. The warp carries appearance but inherits interpolation errors at object boundaries, whereas the tracks show the simulated points directly but sparsely; Sec. 4.2 compares the two paths.

sections.title:
3.4 Renderer
The renderer is a pretrained video model, Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [67] or Ctrl-World [22] initialized from SVD [5],
that receives the first frame of each camera and the three proxy videos, but no text; Ctrl-World, which
natively reads numeric actions, keeps this input in every variant. Each proxy video is encoded by the
renderer’s frozen VAE, concatenated with the noisy latents along channels and read by a widened first layer
whose new weights start at zero, so training starts from the pretrained model. Each token thus carries the
proxy at its own space-time location, and the backbone’s attention relates tokens across space, time and
views. The clean first frame supplies appearance, the warp shows where it goes and the tracks how the
points move; the renderer fills the black regions and synthesizes the real arm, lighting and contact. With
E the VAE encoder and zτ the noisy latents of the future frames at noise level τ , the denoiser computes

sections.title:
4.1 Setup
Data. All models are trained on 326K clips from 41.5K DROID [34] episodes and tested on 1,515 held-out
clips from 900 episodes across 13 labs; 300 validation clips are used only to monitor training. The test clips
come from PointWorld’s test split, so the simulator is not trained on them either. A clip is 21 frames at
15 Hz from the two external cameras, stacked along height at 640×352 per view, with depth and calibration
from PointWorld [26]. No wrist camera and no text are used.
sections.content: 5 Renderers and conditioning variants. We use two renderers and train each with four conditions, each giving it more explicit information than the last: the robots appearance, then the scenes geometry, then the scenes simulated motion. Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [67] (Wan for short) is DiT conditioned on the first frame; we train it with numeric action (8-D end-effector pose and gripper), robot render, robot render plus depth (depth for short), and the point dynamics proxy. The depth condition is second pixel-aligned video that composites the rendered depth of the robot over the depth of the first-frame scene, so it adds the scenes geometry but not its motion (Appendix B). Ctrl-World [22] is an SVD [5] UNet that reads numeric actions through frame-level cross-attention; we retrain it from its SVD initialization in our setting with the numeric action alone and with the same three pixel-aligned conditions added. The effect of point dynamics is always measured between the robot render and the proxy of the same renderer, which differ only in the proxys warp and track videos. Training and inference. Every renderer variant uses the same data, the same global sample order, global batch 32 on 8 A100 GPUs, and 30K steps of full fine-tuning from the renderers pretrained weights (AdamW, learning rate 105, 200 warm-up steps, bfloat16 autocast, no EMA). Each renderer keeps its own noise schedule, first-frame conditioning and VAE. Sampling uses 50 steps without guidance. We report the 30K checkpoint: on the 300 validation clips, every variant with robot render has nearly converged by 20K steps, and the proxy leads the robot render at every 5K checkpoint (Appendix E). On one A100 (batch 1, two views), PointWorld and proxy rendering take 0.93 per clip, next to 17.2 for generating the video with Wan and 30.9 with Ctrl-World; the depth maps are given and not timed. We do not compare against released checkpoints, because most DROID world models require the wrist view and published numbers use different protocols. Metrics. We measure action following by robot error and interaction fidelity by object motion error, our main metric. Both track first-frame query points with CoTracker3 [33] in the real and in the generated video and report the mean pixel distance between the two tracks in the frames where the real track is visible: robot error for up to 150 points inside the robot mask, object motion error for up to 200 points of 10-pixel grid outside the dilated robot mask that move by at least 5 px in the real video. The latter is defined on the test clips with at least 10 such points (1,017 and 1,029 of the 1,515 clips in the two views); large denotes the third with the largest object motion (details in Appendix C). We also report PSNR, LPIPS and FVD, but they are dominated by the background and the robot, and visual realism is known to be poor indicator of physical correctness [50]. Every metric is computed per view and averaged over the two views, and changes are relative differences of the mean error between two variants, computed before rounding. All tables report one training seed per variant; the robot render and the proxy are trained with two more seeds (Sec. 4.2).

sections.title:
4.2 Do point dynamics improve interaction fidelity?
Main comparison. Simulating point dynamics makes object interaction more faithful on both renderers
(Tab. 1). Going from the numeric action to the robot render mostly fixes the robot: robot error drops by
62% on Wan and 58% on Ctrl-World, while object motion error drops by only 13.0% and 9.0%. The point
dynamics proxy lowers object motion error by another 8.6% and 6.2% against the robot render (11.2%
and 8.3% on large motions), more than half of the robot render’s own gain in pixels (0.44 vs. 0.76 and
0.33 vs. 0.52 px). Since CoTracker3 also produces the label point flow, we re-measure with AllTracker [23],
which uses no pseudo-labels: the proxy then lowers object motion error by 11.5% and 7.1%, and SAM 2
object masks [59] agree (Appendix D). On the whole test set, image metrics barely move (PSNR +0.06
and +0.08 dB), and the track error of points that are static in the real video does not rise (0.46 px with
and without the proxy on Wan). In Fig. 3, the models without point dynamics move the arm correctly
but get the object wrong; the proxy gets both right.

sections.title:
4.3 Does the video follow the simulator?
If the renderer reads the point dynamics, rather than redrawing what it would have predicted anyway, its
video should change whenever the simulation changes. We test this at inference by swapping, perturbing
and editing the simulated motion, with the trained renderer fixed.
sections.content: Simulator quality. Better simulators give better videos on both renderers (Fig. 4a). With static points, where every scene point stays in place, object motion error is 49% higher on Wan and 33% higher on Figure 4: The video follows the simulation. Object motion error on the DROID test set when the simulator is swapped (a) or its output perturbed (b) at test time, with the trained renderer fixed. Dots left of the vertical lines (robot render only) are better. Figure 5: Editing the simulated motion steers the video. In this successful example, the simulated motion of the cloth is frozen or doubled at test time, with the robot and the rest of the scene unchanged (Wan2.2). Left: the (edited) point trajectories. 8 Ctrl-World than with PointWorld-large, and higher than with the robot render alone, so the renderer follows the motion it is given. Object motion error then decreases at every step, from hand-written grasp rule to PointWorld-small, PointWorld-large and label point flow itself. The rule is small code simulator: when the gripper closes, the object between the fingers moves rigidly with it until it opens, and everything else stays still. It closes 40% (Wan) and 51% (Ctrl-World) of the gap between static points and PointWorld-large; the rest is pushing, dragging and deformation, which such rule cannot express. PointWorld-large nearly matches label point flow (4.69 vs. 4.66 px on Wan, 4.97 vs. 4.86 px on Ctrl-World). Label point flow is itself estimated from 2D tracks and stereo depth [26], so it is reference, not an upper bound. Perturbations and edits. The renderer also follows changes to the simulators output, whether errors or deliberate edits. On Wan, coherent errors cost far less than incoherent ones (Fig. 4b). Scaling all simulated motion by 0.5 or 1.5, or delaying it by two frames, costs about 510%, whereas independent 2 cm noise on each point costs 33%, because the renderer paints incoherent motion as given. Edits steer the video  (Fig. 5)  : we edit the predicted motion of one object near the gripper in 200 test clips with non-rigid responses, leaving everything else unchanged, and measure the fraction of tracked object points that end closer to the edited than to the original trajectory, on the 5576 clips per edit and view in which the edit moves at least five tracked points. The 200 clips are the non-rigid ones with the largest label motion, and the edited object is the largest connected group of scene points, at 1.5 cm voxels, that PointWorld-large moves by more than 2 cm and that start within 15 cm of the grippers path. When the object is frozen, 61% of its points follow the edit, against 29% for the robot-render model, which does not see the edit, and the proxy models error with respect to the edited trajectory drops from 25.2 px without the edit to 12.8 px. Reversing the horizontal motion or doubling it is followed less often (28% vs. 13% and 19% vs. 13%), as the renderer pulls large, unusual motions back toward what it saw in training. The edits leave the background unchanged and barely affect the robot.

sections.title:
4.4 Point dynamics as input or as an auxiliary loss?
Point dynamics can also reach a video model through an auxiliary training loss on motion [7, 31, 74, 90],
which needs no extra input at inference. We train another Wan variant on the robot render with point
forcing: an auxiliary head on block 15 regresses point tracks from intermediate features during training
and is discarded at inference, following PhysisForcing [90] in its loss weight, head learning rate and
moving-point targets. Its targets are the label point flow, the strongest teacher available. Data, sample
order and budget match the other variants.
sections.content: Both help; here, input helps more. Against the robot render, point forcing lowers object motion error by 3.4% and raises PSNR by 0.06 dB (Tab. 4); with loss weight 1 and the backbones learning rate for the head, it does not help (Appendix G). Giving the simulated dynamics as input lowers object motion error by 8.6%, to 4.69 px against 4.95 px with point forcing. likely reason is what the renderer is asked to do: with forcing it must still infer the scenes response from the robot render, whereas the proxy hands it response computed in 3D. sections.title:
4.5 Real robot
Setup. We collect 300 episodes of 15 tasks on a bimanual setup of two WidowX AI arms, recorded at
30 Hz by a single static RGB-D camera (RealSense D405, 640×480) that looks down on the table. The
tasks cover pick-and-place, stacking, pushing, folding a shirt or a bag, unfolding a bag, and handing a
bag or a pillow from one arm to the other. We calibrate the camera by fitting the rendered URDF to the
robot’s silhouettes and depth, and refine the noisy sensor depth with LingBot-Depth [66]. Label point
flow follows PointWorld [26], with CoTracker3 [33] tracks lifted to 3D with this depth (Appendix H). The
renderer is trained on 270 episodes and tested on 431 clips of 30 held-out episodes (two per task); the
simulator never sees the test clips. We fine-tune PointWorld-large on the label point flow for 6K steps,
which lowers its error on moving test points from 4.05 cm zero-shot to 2.24 cm. Each Wan variant starts
from its DROID model and is fine-tuned for 6K steps with the same recipe on the single view (640×352,
21 frames at 15 Hz). Object motion error is defined on the 265 test clips with moving objects, 89 of them
large.
sections.content: Results. The ordering found on DROID carries over to the real robot (Tab. 5, Fig. 6). Against the numeric action, the robot render lowers robot error by 65% and object motion error by 25%. Against the robot render, the proxy lowers object motion error by another 8.1%, and by 13.4% on large motions, close to the 8.6% and 11.2% on DROID. Against robot render + depth, it lowers object motion error by 4.3%, and by 8.0% on large motions. The gain comes mostly from deformable objects. On the 112 clips of the five bag, cloth and pillow tasks, the proxy lowers object motion error by 12.7% against the robot render 10 and by 7.6% against depth, close to the 12.3% and 8.5% for non-rigid responses on DROID (Tab. 2); on the 153 clips of the other ten tasks it changes object motion error by at most 2.1%. PSNR and LPIPS barely move, while FVD rises from 14.5 to 15.2.

sections.title:
5 Conclusion
Robotic world models that render the robot follow the given action, but still have to guess how the objects
respond. We decouple such a model into a simulator that predicts how 3D scene points respond to the
robot and a renderer that turns the prediction into video, connected by a pixel-aligned point dynamics
proxy. On DROID and on a real robot, explicit point dynamics make object interaction more faithful,
and the generated video follows the simulator and responds to its edits. This suggests that progress in
3D point dynamics, whether learned or written as code, can carry over to robotic world models without
changing how they render.
sections.content: Limitations. The video is only as faithful as the simulation, since the renderer follows plausible simulated motion, errors included. The simulator, in turn, learns from label point flow, which is itself estimated from tracking and depth. Errors thus add up from depth and tracking to the labels, the simulator and the video, and each step leaves room for improvement. The simulator and the renderer are also trained separately, which keeps each replaceable but prevents the renderer from correcting the simulation; training them jointly is promising direction. Sections AC describe the DROID setup, with every setting in Tab. 6. Sec. measures object motion error again with second point tracker and with object masks. Sec. breaks the results down by view, training seed, checkpoint and lab. Sections FH detail the edit experiment, point forcing and the real robot. Simulator and proxy The simulator is PointWorld-large [26], Point Transformer V3 [80] with about 1B parameters, used frozen from its released DROID checkpoint. PointWorld-small, used in Sec. 4.3, is the smaller released DROID checkpoint. The simulator reads the scene points, voxelized at 1.5 cm and described by frozen DINOv3 features [63], together with the gripper points. In single forward pass, it predicts displacements for 10 steps, one every two video frames. It was trained on DROID label point flow, but not on our test clips, which come from the test split of its release. The renderers never see test episode either. Stereo depth and camera calibration also come from PointWorlds DROID release, for training and test alike. For the proxy, the depth map is upsampled to the video resolution of 640352, and every pixel with depth between 0.1 and 3.5 becomes dense scene point. Robot pixels at t=0 are removed with the rendered robot mask, dilated by 77 pixels. The simulator receives only the gripper points, while the proxy renders the full arm from 1M points sampled on its URDF surface. Simulated displacements are interpolated linearly in time to the 15 Hz frame rate. Track points are colored by their initial position, through fixed box of the robot base frame mapped to RGB. Renderers Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [67] reads the proxy through widened patch embedding. Its first latent frame is the clean first frame at timestep zero. The latents of the two views are stacked along height into one token sequence, so tokens attend across views. Ctrl-World [22] reads the proxy through widened input convolution and otherwise keeps its released design, including the first-frame latent concatenation and the cross-attention to numeric actions. Numeric action. On DROID, the numeric action has 8 dimensions: the end-effector position, the sine and cosine of its roll, its pitch, its yaw and the gripper. Each dimension is normalized by the 1st and 99th percentiles of the training set. Ctrl-World reads it in every variant, through its action cross-attention. Wan reads it only in the numeric-action variant. There, the actions of the four video frames in each latent frame are concatenated, and two-layer MLP maps them to an offset of that latent frames time embedding. The last layer of this MLP starts at zero. In every Wan variant, the text cross-attention receives the embedding of an empty prompt. Depth variant. The robot render + depth variant (depth for short) adds one video per camera to the robot render, encoded like the proxy videos. Its first two channels hold the z-buffer depth of the rendered robot in each frame and the depth of the dense first-frame scene points. Five of the 15 tasks put objects in place: all food on plate, cake on yellow plate, an eggplant into white box, lemon into blue bowl and red cuboid on green plate. Two push green bowl to purple bowl and green cube to blue cube. Three stack purple bowl in blue bowl, red cube on green cube and three bowls. The other five fold black bag and red shirt in half, unfold black bag, and hand black bag or U-shaped pillow from one arm to the other. Each task has 20 episodes, 176K frames in total. The robot state is the 14-D joint state of the two arms (six joints and gripper each). Calibration. No camera calibration was recorded, so we estimate it. RGB and depth share the optical center, since free translation between them converges to 4 mm. The principal point of the depth image, however, is about 11 pixels lower, so we reproject depth onto the RGB grid. In 360 frames, we render the arm from the URDF at the logged joint state. The focal length, principal point and camera pose are fitted jointly to the arms silhouettes and to the depth on its pixels. The fitted focal length is about 380 pixels and varies by 0.7% across three disjoint subsets of frames. On held-out frames, the depth error on robot pixels is 1718 mm and the silhouette IoU is 0.760.77. Depth. At about 1 m, the raw sensor depth on the dark tablecloth fluctuates by centimeters. We compared raw and filtered sensor depth with MoGe-2 [72] aligned to the sensor and with LingBot-Depth [66], which takes RGB and raw depth, on 232 held-out windows of training episodes. Three measures score them: the 23 median depth error on robot pixels against the rendered robot, the frame-to-frame jitter of static points, and the change of pairwise distances between points on carried rigid objects. LingBot-Depth gives 17.9, 12.1 and 4.0 mm against 17.8, 27.7 and 8.1 mm for raw depth, while MoGe-2 places the arm 85 mm off. We therefore use LingBot-Depth for the labels, the simulators input points and the depth condition. Label point flow. We follow PointWorlds labeling [26]. CoTracker3 [33] is queried on dense 3-pixel grid in the first frame, excluding robot pixels. Each track is lifted to 3D with the median depth of its 55 neighborhood on the same surface. In every frame, points hidden by the arm, found with the rendered robot mask, are marked invisible and not supervised in that frame. Outliers are removed with PointWorlds DBSCAN filter. Two changes account for the single overhead camera. First, the depth jitter of static points (12 mm) exceeds the 5 mm per-step scale of PointWorlds motion weighting. Static points are therefore pinned to their first-frame position and supervised only in frames where they are visible. Second, held object is often hidden by the gripper. Points whose observed motion follows the gripper are attached to it. The other points of the same object move with them, by the objects rigid motion fitted per frame with the Kabsch algorithm. In frames where these points are occluded, they are filled in with that rigid motion. Points with contradictory evidence, such as depth change without 2D motion, are left unsupervised after the first frame. Simulator. We start from the released PointWorld-large checkpoint used on DROID and feed it the points of the single camera. The state normalization is that of the DROID release, with the gripper statistics applied to both grippers. It is fine-tuned on 8 GPUs with global batch 32 and learning rate 105 for 6K steps, and all other settings follow the release.
